newsitem.title: USA: Group sees decline in emerging market investment.
newsitem.headline: Group sees decline in emerging market investment.

text.p: Private capital flows to emerging economies are expected to level off this year because an increase in U.S. interest rates may draw money away from hot markets in developing countries, the Institute of international Finance said Tuesday.
The Institute, a global association of financial organisations, estimated that net capital investment would slow slightly to $249 billion from $255.1 billion last year and $256.6 billion in 1995.

Officials also explained in a briefing for reporters that last year's numbers were buoyed by Mexico's financing used to help the country repay early its debt to the United States accumulated as a result of an economic rescue package that followed the crash of Mexico's peso.
"Without this, the estimates for this year would show an increase," an officical said.

Stock market investment in emerging economies, however, should continue to show impressive performance, the Institute said, going from $100.6 billion in 1995 to $112.5 billion in 1996 and an estimated $117 billion this year. Stock activity accounts for nearly half of total flows.
In the briefing, IIF Managing Director Charles Dallara said industrial governments, emerging market economies, multilateral institutions and others must work to sustain net private capital flows.
"Not withstanding the positive trends evident, there are some posssible risks to sustaining private capital flows at this time," he said.
These include uneven industrial country performance, a slackening of reforms in emerging market economies, diminished influence of multilateral institutions and "some injudicious lending."

The institute also issued a letter to the International Monetary Fund's powerful Interim Committee saying that sound, coordinated policies by industrial countries are essential for a healthy world economy and growing exports for emerging market economies.

The letter sent in conjunction with the semi-annual meeting of the IMF and World Bank, which begins this week, said sustained higher growth in Europe would require careful management of government spending with sound monetary policy.
It said Japan should implement its programme of market deregulation while confronting the weakness of its financial sector.
For its part, The United States must cope with the apparent strength of its economy without allowing inflationary pressures to rise or the expansion to be stifled, the financial group said.
